meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.direction_justification: Cessation or switching of antidiabetic therapies due to emerging side effects was treated as a competing risk rather than an intermediate post-exposure event, potentially distorting rate ratios.

findings.title: Competing risk specification for transient side effects
findings.mechanism: Treating acute adverse symptoms (such as diarrhea, emesis, dizziness) as competing risks rather than time-varying mediators or censoring events may alter cause-specific risk estimates.
evidence: Competing events systematically defined by any incidence of specific acute symptoms including diarrhea/emesis, acne, dizziness, arrhythmia

findings.title: Extensive missingness in key laboratory markers
findings.mechanism: Because over 90% of patients lacked baseline HbA1c and >30% lacked BMI or FPG, the propensity score matching could not balance these major determinants of diabetic complications.

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: Patients on newer, high-cost injectable medications are subject to closer clinical monitoring and laboratory investigations, increasing the detection rate of subclinical or incidental conditions (e.g., thyroid nodules, benign dysfunction, acute nephritis).

findings.title: Surveillance and ascertainment bias
findings.mechanism: Outcomes were identified via ICD-10 codes and regular expression keyword matching in routine health records without secondary adjudication or chart review, making findings sensitive to differential medical contact and testing.
evidence: Combination of ICD-10 diagnosis, discharge diagnosis, imaging diagnosis, and regular expression for terminology recognition was applied (Table 2S)

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: Multiple outcomes and multiple sub-analyses (by duration, individual drug agent, and comparator) were performed without a pre-registered protocol or correction for multiplicity.

findings.title: Multiplicity of safety endpoints without pre-registration
findings.mechanism: Testing over 15 distinct clinical endpoints across multiple comparison groups and duration subgroups without family-wise error control increases the risk of false-positive associations.
evidence: Extensive array of outcomes assessed across 4 separate GLP-1 RA agents and two comparator groups without documented pre-analysis protocol

overall.summary: This retrospective observational cohort study reports increased hazard ratios for multiple adverse outcomes (including pancreatitis, acute nephritis, renal failure, and thyroid cancer) among GLP-1 RA users compared to metformin and insulin users. However, the study is subject to high risk of bias from confounding by indication, extreme missingness in key metabolic and glycemic indicators (HbA1c missing in >90% of participants, BMI and FPG missing in >30%), and selection bias resulting from defining cohorts based on longitudinal monotherapy persistence. Surveillance bias and testing of multiple unadjudicated electronic health record endpoints further inflate observed effect estimates away from the null.

adjusted_effect.outcome: Pancreatitis (<12 months GLP-1 RAs vs metformin-only after PSM)

unresolvable_without_more_data: Raw 2x2 event counts and person-time per outcome were not reported in the text or tables, precluding independent calculation of absolute risk differences and incidence rates.
